newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia study says EMU may be good for gold.
newsitem.headline: Australia study says EMU may be good for gold.

text.p: European Monetary Union (EMU) may reduce the importance of the U.S. dollar in world trade and brighten gold's image as an international reserve asset, according to a gold industry study released on Sunday.

Rather than pry gold from the vaults of central banks, a single currency among European nations could actually make gold a more prized possession, according to a study by Australia-based AME Mineral Economics Ltd.
Fears of significant reductions in official holdings of gold by European central banks in the event of monetary union were groundless, said the study, "Gold 1997-Costs Under Pressure."

"It is much more likely that the participants in the EMU will hang on to their gold in order to enhance the perceived strength of the euro (European currency) in international markets," the report said.
The central banks' main influence on the gold market is through gold lending, which has been part of the boom in derivatives trading, AME said.
A single European currency, the euro, is expected to be launched on January 1, 1999.
A new-found lust for gold among Europe's leading economies could be repeated elsewhere as members of other trading groups peg their currencies against each other, AME said.
"A de facto return to a system or several systems of fixed exchange rates can only enhance the use of gold as an independent reserve asset," AME said.
Any actual sales of gold by central banks would reflect how the precious metal sized up on bank balance sheets, AME said.
"Future central bank gold sales will depend on official attitudes to gold's contribution to the risk and return of central bank portfolios," AME said.
Without providing specific figures, AME estimated that about one-third of all the gold in the world is held by central banks and international financial institutions.
Industry estimates put the central bank and financial institution gold hoard at around 35,000 tonnes, equal to 10 years of world production.

Gold reserves have for many years been moving out of the traditional gold-holding countries to economies which have consistently higher growth in trade and incomes, AME said. Such movement was now occurring towards East Asia, the study said.

"The East-Asian take-up of official gold will continue and should spread to South Asian countries, such as India, and the former east bloc countries as they integrate themselves into the world economy," AME said.
